title: Vāsudeva and Saṅkarṣaṇa were honoured by patrons from the Indo-Greek world to the Deccan before the epics reached their final form
body:
Four independent kinds of evidence cluster within roughly a century and a half: coins of the Greco-Bactrian king Agathocles found at Aï Khanoum (c. 190–180 BCE) showing two deities with a plough and a wheel; the Besnagar pillar on which Heliodorus, envoy of an Indo-Greek king, calls himself a Bhāgavata and Vāsudeva the “god of gods”; the Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions in Rajasthan naming Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva together; and the Nāṇeghāṭ inscription of the Sātavāhana queen Nāganikā invoking them in the western Deccan.

The patrons were a Greek king, a Greek envoy, a local ruler and a Deccan queen. Whatever the date of the Mahābhārata’s final redaction, devotion to these two figures was already geographically and socially wide.
caveat: The inscriptions name Vāsudeva and Saṅkarṣaṇa, not “Kṛṣṇa”. The coin figures are identified with them by interpretation (class 5), and coins found at Aï Khanoum do not by themselves show worship there. Identifying the inscriptional gods with the epic Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma is also scholarly interpretation. None of this dates the Kṛṣṇa narratives or proves any event in them.

title: A grammarian attests devotion to Vāsudeva and Arjuna, and a later one the staging of Kṛṣṇa’s and Bali’s stories
body:
Pāṇini’s rule 4.3.98 (vāsudevārjunābhyāṃ vun) forms words for devotees of Vāsudeva and of Arjuna — evidence that both were objects of bhakti when the rule was framed, usually dated c. 5th–4th c. BCE. Two centuries or so later, Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya on 3.1.26 describes performers who “have Kaṃsa killed” and “have Bali bound” before the audience’s eyes, and on 2.2.24 and 2.2.34 alludes to Kṛṣṇa with Saṅkarṣaṇa and to a prāsāda of Rāma and Keśava.

Read alongside the Ṛgveda’s three strides of Viṣṇu (1.154) and the Śatapatha’s dwarf who wins the earth (ŚB 1.2.5, with no Bali), the grammarians supply a textual stage of the Vāmana–Bali story between the Veda and the Purāṇas.
caveat: These are grammatical examples: they attest that stories and cults were current, not the contents or date of any surviving epic or Purāṇa. Patañjali names neither Viṣṇu nor Vāmana in the Bali example, and reading “Rāma” as Balarāma is interpretation.

sources.locator: Mahābhāṣya on Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.26, vārttika 6 (Kielhorn ed. II.34–36)
sources.quote: kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe kaṃsaṃ ghātayati … balibandham ācaṣṭe baliṃ bandhayati

title: The oldest physical witness to the Mahābhārata is a table of contents found in a Buddhist anthology on the Silk Road
body:
The Spitzer manuscript — Sanskrit fragments recovered at Kizil in the Tarim Basin in 1906 and now divided between Berlin and London — contains a list of the Mahābhārata’s parvans. Radiocarbon dating puts it around 130 CE (80–230 CE); palaeography suggests c. 200–230. It is roughly a millennium older than any surviving manuscript of the epic’s text.

The list was copied far from the Gaṅgā plain, in a Buddhist philosophical compilation, which says something about how widely the epic’s structure was known by the 2nd–3rd century.
caveat: A parvan list shows that a work of that shape existed, not the wording of its text; the list’s gaps may reflect the purpose of the list rather than the epic’s contents.

title: A 7th-century inscription dates itself by the Bhārata war — and fixes the latest possible date of Kālidāsa
body:
The Aihole praśasti of Pulakeśin II, composed by Ravikīrti, is dated both in the Śaka era (556, i.e. 634/635 CE) and as 3,735 years after the Bhārata war — a reckoning that corresponds to the traditional Kali-yuga epoch of 3102 BCE, which Āryabhaṭa had already used in 499 CE. The same poem names Kālidāsa and Bhāravi as poets of renown.

One stone thus shows a traditional cosmological era in practical use by a Deccan court, and gives literary history a firm terminus ante quem for two poets.
caveat: The epoch is a traditional, astronomically computed reckoning. Its use in 634 CE is evidence for how 7th-century elites counted time, not for when — or whether — the war took place.

sources.quote: attained to the fame of Kâḷidâsa and of Bhâravi

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

title: A verse of the Devī Māhātmya was carved in stone in 608 CE
body:
The Dadhimatī Mātā inscription (Gupta year 289, 608 CE) quotes a verse beginning sarva-maṅgala-māṅgalye, found in the Devī Māhātmya (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 91.9). It gives that hymn a secure latest date — rare for a Purāṇic text. Nearly two centuries earlier the Gangdhar inscription (423/424 CE) records a “terrifying abode of the divine Mothers” built beside a temple of Viṣṇu.

Together they put organised Goddess worship on the epigraphic record well before the oldest manuscripts of the texts that celebrate it.
caveat: The quotation shows that one verse existed by 608 CE, not that the whole Devī Māhātmya did in its present form.

title: From Kaniṣka onward, the Kuṣāṇa “Śiva” on coins is labelled with an Iranian name
body:
Gold coins of Kaniṣka I and his successors label a trident-bearing, bull-associated deity ΟΗϷΟ (Oesho) in Bactrian — a name many numismatists derive from the Iranian wind god Vāyu (Vēš). Wima Kadphises’ earlier coins show a similar deity with no name label, and a Kharoṣṭhī legend calling the king a devotee of Maheśvara. The graph keeps Oesho as its own record with two disputed IDENTIFIED_WITH assertions — to Śiva and to Vāyu — and the evidence for and against.

The case shows why identity must be an assertion rather than a merge: the same image can belong to two traditions at once, or be a deliberate synthesis.
caveat: This is a live scholarly dispute; the dataset records both readings and does not decide it.

title: The most-cited “earliest image of Śiva” is the least secure item in the graph
body:
The Mohenjo-daro seal that John Marshall in 1931 called “proto-Śiva” is the oldest object in the dataset associated with Śiva — c. 2350–2000 BCE. It is also modelled as a disputed claim: Doris Srinivasan’s iconological assessment and later work argue that the horned, seated figure does not support the identification, and the Indus script remains undeciphered.

The atlas therefore does not use the disputed seal identification for Śiva’s “earliest attestation”: his earliest dated material record in the profile is the Gudimallam liṅga, whose dates (from the 3rd c. BCE to the 3rd c. CE) are themselves disputed; the majority view places it in the 2nd–1st c. BCE.
caveat: Absence of a secure identification is not evidence that no continuity exists; it means the seal cannot carry the weight popular accounts place on it.

title: In the Mahābhārata the fish that saves Manu is Brahmā, not Viṣṇu
body:
The flood story runs from the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.8.1, where an unnamed fish saves Manu) to the Purāṇas. In the critical Mahābhārata (3.185.48) the fish reveals itself as Prajāpati Brahmā. In the Purāṇas — the Matsya (1–2), the Agni (2) and the Bhāgavata (8.24) — the fish is Viṣṇu, and in ten-avatāra lists such as Agni Purāṇa 49 it stands first; the Bhāgavata adds the demon Hayagrīva who steals the Veda.

The theological identity of the rescuer changed as the story moved between bodies of literature; the graph keeps each version separate and joins them with a DERIVED_FROM assertion rather than a merge.
caveat: A later Vaiṣṇava reading may preserve older oral tradition; textual sequence is not proof of origin.

sources.quote: ahaṃ prajāpatir brahmā matparaṃ nādhigamyate / matsyarūpeṇa yūyaṃ ca mayāsmān mokṣitā bhayāt

title: There is no single early list of Viṣṇu’s ten avatāras
body:
The constituted text of the Mahābhārata’s Nārāyaṇīya lists Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma and others — but no Fish, no Tortoise and no Kalki. The Agni Purāṇa’s iconographic list of ten (AgP 49) includes Balarāma rather than Kṛṣṇa; the Bhāgavata counts twenty-two; the Matsya includes figures such as Māndhātṛ and Vyāsa.

The familiar ten is a convention that crystallised late. Every AVATARA_OF edge in the graph is qualified by the text that makes it, so the lists can be compared rather than flattened.
caveat: Vulgate texts and other passages of the same works sometimes count differently; the comparison uses the critical or e-text editions cited.

sources.edition: Rajendralal Mitra ed. (Bibliotheca Indica 1870–79); GRETIL e-text

title: In the critical Viṣṇu Purāṇa, the word “mahāpurāṇa” is an insertion
body:
The critical text of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (3.6.21–23) lists eighteen purāṇas. The half-verse that calls them mahāpurāṇas and adds the upapurāṇas appears only as a starred insertion (3.6.23*8), recorded in the apparatus rather than the constituted text.

The category “the Eighteen Mahāpurāṇas” — the frame through which the corpus is usually introduced — is itself something the manuscripts show being added.
caveat: An insertion in one text attests manuscript variation, not a date for the term; other Purāṇas use it.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

title: The critical Mahābhārata has no prayer to Kṛṣṇa when Draupadī is disrobed
body:
In the constituted text (2.61.40–41) Draupadī’s garments simply keep appearing as Duḥśāsana pulls. Her famous appeal to Govinda “who dwells in Dvārakā” survives only in star passages (*542–*547) relegated to the apparatus of the Critical Edition.

The graph records Draupadī DEVOTEE_OF Kṛṣṇa at this point as disputed, with the comparison table showing exactly what each source states.
caveat: The Critical Edition reconstructs the archetype shared by the manuscripts it used; it does not show the prayer is late everywhere, and many living tellings centre on it.

title: The Mahābhārata tells its own Rāma story — with Lakṣmaṇa killing Kumbhakarṇa and no fire ordeal
body:
The Rāmopākhyāna (MBh (CE) 3.257–275) retells the Rāma story differently from Vālmīki: Lakṣmaṇa, not Rāma, kills Kumbhakarṇa (3.271.16, against VR (CE) 6.55.128–129); Sītā is cleared by the gods’ testimony and a curse on Rāvaṇa rather than by entering fire; there is no banishment. Yet it already presents Rāma as Viṣṇu descended (3.260.5).

Two Sanskrit tellings of the same story, in two great texts, disagree on who kills whom — exactly the kind of difference the comparison tables exist to show.
caveat: Whether the Rāmopākhyāna abridges Vālmīki or preserves an independent version is disputed.

sources.quote: tadartham avatīrṇo 'sau manniyogāc caturbhujaḥ / viṣṇuḥ praharatāṃ śreṣṭhaḥ

title: The Upaniṣad that first makes Śiva the supreme lord is built from older Rudra verses
body:
The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad reuses Ṛgvedic and Yajurvedic material verbatim — the Śatarudrīya of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (ŚvU 3.5), a Ṛgvedic verse to Rudra (RV 1.114.8 = ŚvU 4.22) and the Puruṣa hymn (RV 10.90.1–2 = ŚvU 3.14–15) — while applying śiva and maheśvara to one supreme lord.

The passage from Vedic Rudra to the Śiva of devotion is visible here in the texture of a single text, not only in a sequence of texts.
caveat: Whether śiva is a name or an epithet in these verses is debated; the identification of Rudra with Śiva is recorded as the Upaniṣad’s assertion.

title: The Gaṅgā is almost absent from the Ṛgveda
body:
The river at the heart of later sacred geography appears once by name in the Ṛgveda, in the river list of 10.75.5 (with the adjective gāṅgya at 6.45.31). The Sarasvatī has hymns of its own. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.4.1) Agni’s eastward journey runs from the Sarasvatī to Videha beyond the Sadānīrā.

The sacred map of the earliest texts and the sacred map of the temple atlas are different maps.
caveat: Absence of mention in one corpus is not absence of the river from the composers’ world; the migration reading of ŚB 1.4.1 is interpretive.

title: Vedic prose already names the Mahābhārata’s frame figures
body:
The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (13.5.4) names Janamejaya Pārikṣita, who performed the horse sacrifice, with brothers Bhīmasena, Ugrasena and Śrutasena — the trio the epic names at its opening — and Bharata Dauḥṣanti, “whom the apsaras Śakuntalā bore”.

The epic’s royal frame draws on names already present in Vedic memory of the Kuru realm.
caveat: That the Brāhmaṇa’s Janamejaya and the epic’s are the same figure is inferred from names and lineage, not proven; and a shared name says nothing about the historicity of the epic’s war.

title: Both oldest Upaniṣads credit the doctrine of rebirth to a king — and tell it differently
body: The “five fires” teaching on the fate of the dead is given to the brahmin Uddālaka Āruṇi by the Pañcāla king Pravāhaṇa Jaivali in both the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2) and the Chāndogya (5.3–5.10). Only the Chāndogya ties rebirth to conduct and to birth in a social class; the Bṛhadāraṇyaka quotes a Ṛgvedic verse instead.
caveat: This is a literary attribution, not evidence that the doctrine originated among kṣatriyas.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)
Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

title: Whose daughter is Sītā? The answer depends on the tradition
body:
In Vālmīki she is found in a furrow and raised by Janaka. In the Buddhist Dasaratha Jātaka she is Rāma’s sister and becomes his queen. In Vimalasūri’s Jain Paumacariya she is Janaka’s natural daughter with a twin brother, Bhāmaṇḍala. In several tellings — Guṇabhadra’s Jain Uttarapurāṇa, the Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa, the Thai Ramakien and the Lao Phra Lak Phra Lam — she is born in Rāvaṇa’s household (to Mandodarī or to Rāvaṇa); in some, such as the Ramakien, an omen leads to her being set adrift, in others she is buried or abandoned and found by Janaka.

The graph records each parentage as a separate kinship assertion qualified by its text, so the genealogy view shows all of them at once.
caveat: Several rows still carry “awaiting check” locators; no line of descent between the tellings is implied, and no version is treated as the authentic one.

sources.quote: the daughter’s name was the lady Sītā

title: In later devotional tellings, the Sītā whom Rāvaṇa abducts is a reflection
body:
Vālmīki’s Rāvaṇa seizes Sītā. Kampaṉ’s Rāvaṇa lifts the earth on which her hermitage stands, so as not to touch her. In the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa and Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas the real Sītā enters fire before the abduction and an illusory Sītā (Māyā-Sītā) is taken; the ordeal by fire restores the original.

The change follows the theology: as Rāma becomes Brahman itself, his consort cannot be touched by the demon.
caveat: The motif is older than the Mānas and is not unique to it; the theological explanation is a scholarly reading.

sources.quote: तुम्ह पावक महुँ करहु निवासा। जौ लगि करौं निसाचर नासा ॥

title: A Thai royal ceremony is named after two Tamil temple hymns
body:
The Bangkok court Brahmans’ new-year rite Triyampawai–Trippawai takes its name from Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai and Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai — Tamil hymns to Śiva and to Viṣṇu sung in the month of Mārkaḻi. Tamil texts in Thai and Grantha scripts survive, and the hymns have been recorded being chanted.

It is a living thread from South Indian bhakti to a Southeast Asian court, distinct from the better-known Rāmāyaṇa route.
caveat: This does not date the transmission, or show that the officiants understand the Tamil they recite.

title: A 16th-century poet produced a corrected edition of a Marathi classic
body:
The Jñāneśvarī carries its own dated colophon (Śaka 1212, 1290 CE, under the Yādava king Rāmacandra) and a second note, dated 1584, in which Eknāth says he restored the text because variant readings had corrupted it.

The problem of textual corruption — and a deliberate attempt to correct it — appears in a vernacular tradition centuries before modern critical editions.
caveat: The e-text used is a modern edition; the colophons themselves should be checked against early manuscripts.

sources.quote: एकाजनार्दनें अत्यादरीं| गीता- ज्ञानेश्वरी प्रतिशुद्ध केली

title: The oldest Tamil grammar names Māyōṉ and Cēyōṉ as lords of landscapes without myth; other Caṅkam poems already give them Viṣṇu’s and Skanda’s stories, and the medieval commentator glosses them so
body:
The Tolkāppiyam names Māyōṉ (“the dark one”) and Cēyōṉ (“the red one”) as presiding over the forest and mountain landscapes of love poetry. Other Caṅkam poems, such as the Paripāṭal hymns to Tirumāl, already attach Viṣṇu–Kṛṣṇa mythology to Māyōṉ; the medieval commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar glosses the pair as Viṣṇu and Murukaṉ; and Murukaṉ’s identification with the Sanskrit Skanda is a further convergence.

The graph keeps Murukaṉ and Skanda as two records joined by an assertion qualified by tradition — the convergence is part of the history, not an assumption.
caveat: The date of the relevant part of the Tolkāppiyam is itself disputed.

title: 43 of the 70 temples with founding legends stand in buildings dated after 1500 CE
body:
Of the 70 temples in the atlas whose tradition gives a founding story, 43 stand in a main building dated after 1500 CE (counting the surviving structure, or the latest construction where a site was rebuilt; renovations do not count) — among them Kāśī Viśvanātha temple (1780), Kālīghāṭ temple (1798), Viṣṇupada temple (1787), Badrīnātha temple (1803). Across all 238 dated temples, 16 have a main building from before 600 CE by this rule, and several of those — Deogarh, Udayagiri, Bhitargaon, Tigawa — are monuments no longer in regular worship.

Many of the places most central to living practice have been rebuilt repeatedly, while some of the oldest fabric survives where worship lapsed. The atlas therefore keeps two dates on every temple: the tradition’s and the building’s.
caveat: A late building is not a late cult: inscriptions, texts and earlier phases may attest worship long before the surviving fabric. The counts describe the 103 temples of this dataset only, and one early date (Muṇḍeśvarī) is disputed.

title: One 18th-century queen stands behind the present fabric of several ancient shrines
body:
Ahilyābāī Holkar of Indore built the present Kāśī Viśvanātha temple (1780) and the Viṣṇupada at Gaya (1787), a separate Somanātha temple beside the old site (1783), and renovated Aundha Nāganātha; a role at Grishneshwar is disputed.

At Kāśī and Gaya the buildings pilgrims enter today are hers; at Somnath the main temple is the one completed in 1951.
caveat: These are rebuildings and renovations of existing sacred sites, not foundations; the Grishneshwar attribution is disputed.

title: The twelve jyotirliṅgas are a fixed list with unfixed places
body:
Four of the twelve positions have rival claimant temples — Vaidyanātha (Deoghar or Parli), Nāgeśvara (Dwarka, Aundha or Jageshwar), and others — and at least seven of the fifteen claimant temples in the atlas are buildings of 1700 or later.

The network is real as a devotional list; its geography is contested in ways the map makes visible.
caveat: Several memberships rest on recall-level sources; a late building does not mean a late cult.

title: Conquest carried a temple design from Kanchi to Pattadakal
body:
After the Cālukya king Vikramāditya II took the Pallava capital Kanchi, his queen Lokamahādevī built the Virūpākṣa at Pattadakal (c. 740–745), whose Drāviḍa design follows Kanchi’s Kailāsanātha. A century earlier the Pallava Narasiṃhavarman I had taken the Cālukya capital Vātāpi.

The atlas’s DERIVED_FROM edge between two temples records an argument about influence, with its evidence class.
caveat: Stylistic dependence is a scholarly argument (class 5), not a documented commission.

title: One Vaiṣṇava family at Eran kept its cult under a change of empire
body:
At Eran, Dhanyaviṣṇu’s family raised a pillar under the Gupta Budhagupta (484/85 CE) and then the colossal Varāha under the Hūṇa ruler Toramāṇa (c. 510), dating the new foundation by Toramāṇa’s first regnal year.

The inscriptions show local patrons sustaining a Vaiṣṇava cult across a political rupture.
caveat: The pillar names Mātṛviṣṇu and his younger brother Dhanyaviṣṇu (lines 7–9 of the edition, now verified); continuity of a cult under a new overlord says nothing about the overlord’s own religion.

sources.locator: Eran Pillar Inscription of the time of Budhagupta, lines 1–9

title: The epics were carved in stone in Java and Cambodia as monumental programmes
body:
Prambanan’s Rāmāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇa reliefs belong to a temple tied to the Śivagṛha inscription of 856 CE — the same period as the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (c. 856–930). Angkor Wat, built under Sūryavarman II (c. 1113–1150), carries the churning of the ocean, the Kurukṣetra battle and the war in Laṅkā in its galleries.

Some of the most extensive surviving narrative programmes of these stories in stone stand outside South Asia.
caveat: The link between Prambanan and the Śivagṛha inscription is an argument (de Casparis), since the inscription was found apart from the temple; the comparison of scale is a statement about what survives, not a measurement made here.

sources.locator: Angkor (site page not reachable during research)

title: The oldest Tamil reference to Ōṇam makes it Māyōṉ’s festival, in Madurai
body:
The Caṅkam poem Maduraikkāñci (lines 590–591), describing Pāṇḍya Madurai, calls Ōṇam the festival of Māyōṉ “who overcame the crowding asuras” — the dark god of the Tamil landscapes later identified with Viṣṇu. The poem names no Bali, though a Māyōṉ who defeats asuras can be read as Vāmana overcoming Bali, and Tiruvōṇam is Vāmana’s birth-asterism. The story most Keralites tell today — the yearly return of the generous king Mahābali — is the festival’s dominant living tradition.

The graph keeps both: the early textual attestation of the festival’s god, and the living association with Bali, each with its own evidence class.
caveat: The date of the Maduraikkāñci is itself disputed, and a poem about Madurai does not show what the festival meant elsewhere. It neither names nor excludes Bali; the Mahābali association is recorded as tradition (class 6), and nothing here shows it to be a later invention.

title: One Purāṇic passage already gives Holī two origin stories
body:
Nārada Purāṇa 1.124 describes the Holī rite and names Holikā, the demoness who tried to burn the child Prahlāda, as the figure whose burning it re-enacts; the same passage also ties the night to Śiva burning Kāma. A Bhaviṣyottara text quoted by the medieval digest-writer Hemādri gives a third figure, the ogress Ḍhauṇḍhā.

The festival’s explanations were plural as soon as texts explain it, and the graph links each one to the passage that gives it.
caveat: The Nārada Purāṇa is late and layered, so the passage dates the explanation only loosely. The earliest references to Holākā that Kane lists (the Pūrvamīmāṃsā’s Holākādhikaraṇa, the Kāṭhaka Gṛhya) give no origin story at all; the festival may be older than any text that explains it.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, p. 238: Bhaviṣyottara ch. 132, quoted by Hemādri

title: The Raghuvaṃśa names Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa
body:
Cantos 10–15 of Kālidāsa’s Raghuvaṃśa retell the Rāma story. At 15.63–64, inside the story, Rāma’s sons Kuśa and Lava, urged by their teacher, sing “the Rāmāyaṇa first composed by Prācetasa” — Vālmīki; at 1.4 the poet thanks the “earlier poets” who opened the way. That these cantos follow Vālmīki is an inference from the retelling, but the poem knows his work by name.

With the Aihole inscription of 634 CE, which names Kālidāsa, it brackets the Rāmāyaṇa’s standing as a classic in the mid-first millennium.
caveat: The naming is an event in the narrative, not the poet’s statement of his source, and Aśvaghoṣa’s Buddhacarita (1.43, Vālmīki “first created verse”) is an earlier witness to Vālmīki’s fame. Kālidāsa’s own date is disputed (usually c. 4th–5th c. CE); the verses show the text he knew existed, not which recension it was.

sources.quote: vṛttaṃ rāmasya vālmīkeḥ kṛtis tau kiṃnarasvanau
attained to the fame of Kâḷidâsa and of Bhâravi

title: A book printed as part of the Skanda Purāṇa belongs, by its manuscripts, to the Vāyu Purāṇa
body:
The Revā-khaṇḍa — the glorification of the Narmadā printed as Skanda Purāṇa 5.3 — survives in two different works. One, according to the manuscript evidence assembled by its editor, belongs to the Vāyu Purāṇa, though printed editions place it in the Skanda. The graph keeps both texts and both attributions.

The Purāṇas are open, layered collections; the boundaries of “a Purāṇa” are themselves a product of manuscripts and printers.
caveat: This rests on the editor’s note in the e-text and the manuscript study it reports; the printed colophons still name the Skanda Purāṇa.

sources.edition: Revākhaṇḍa printed as SkP 5.3 (Veṅkaṭeśvara 1910); GRETIL e-text by J. Neuss, who assigns it to the Vāyupurāṇa

title: The six categories of Vaiśeṣika are stated in Praśastapāda, not in the critically edited sūtras
body:
Vaiśeṣika is known for its six categories (padārthas) — substance, quality, action, universal, particularity and inherence. In the e-text of the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra used here, no sūtra lists all six; they are set out by Praśastapāda (c. 6th c. CE), who also opens his work with homage to Īśvara.

The classical system, in other words, is partly the commentator’s.
caveat: Recensions of the sūtras differ: the commonly printed text (with Śaṅkara Miśra’s commentary) has a sūtra listing six categories, which the critically edited recension lacks. The finding is about that recension.

title: Java dated its own Mahābhārata: the Bhāratayuddha was finished in 1157
body:
The Old Javanese poem Bhāratayuddha, a free recasting of the epic’s war books, gives its own date by a chronogram (1157 CE). Mpu Sedah began it and Mpu Panuluh completed it for King Jayabhaya of Kediri. An earlier Old Javanese prose rendering of the Virāṭaparvan records a recital in 996.

Few Sanskrit retellings of the epic can be dated so exactly as this Javanese one.
caveat: A chronogram dates the poem’s completion as the poets state it; the Javanese version reshapes the story and is not a translation.

title: Thirteen plays found in Kerala in 1909 are “Bhāsa’s” by argument, not by signature
body:
The Trivandrum plays, published from manuscripts found in Kerala in the early 20th century, include the epic dramas Ūrubhaṅga, Dūtavākya, Karṇabhāra and the Pratimā and Abhiṣeka plays. They are attributed to Bhāsa, the dramatist Kālidāsa and Bāṇa (c. 640 CE) praise; the plays themselves do not name an author.

The graph records the attribution as a debated claim with the evidence for and against, while still connecting each play to the epic episodes it dramatises.
caveat: Many scholars accept the attribution for some or all of the plays; others think they are later Kerala stage versions. The dataset does not decide.

title: Śiva receiving the Gaṅgā is carved at Udayagiri a century before Elephanta
body:
The Gaṅgādhara form — Śiva catching the descending Gaṅgā in his hair — is best known from the great panel in Elephanta Cave 1 (6th c.). In the graph its earliest dated representation is beside the doorway of Udayagiri Cave 6, in the early 5th century under Candragupta II.

Linking each iconographic form to its earliest dated image turns the story’s spread into a visible sequence.
caveat: The identification of the Udayagiri figure rests on art-historical description checked against reference works; earliest dated in the graph is not earliest made.

title: Two early image manuals disagree on Varuṇa’s mount
body:
Varāhamihira’s Bṛhat Saṃhitā (6th c.) and the Agni Purāṇa’s image chapters agree closely on many prescriptions — the eight-armed Viṣṇu’s weapons almost word for word — but give Varuṇa different mounts: a goose in one, the sea-creature makara in the other.

Iconography was prescribed by texts, and the texts themselves varied; the comparison table sets them side by side.
caveat: Both texts are layered and their image chapters are hard to date; other early prescriptions (the Viṣṇudharmottara, the Matsya Purāṇa) are not compared here, so nothing is claimed about which manual is oldest. Images in stone follow neither text consistently.

title: The oldest Devī Māhātmya manuscript in the graph is four centuries younger than its verse in stone
body:
A palm-leaf manuscript of the Devī Māhātmya in the Schøyen Collection (MS 2174) dates to the 11th century. A verse of the same hymn was already carved in the Dadhimatī Mātā inscription of 608 CE.

For many Purāṇic texts the stone record is older than any surviving manuscript — another reason the atlas keeps textual, manuscript and epigraphic dates apart.
caveat: The 11th-century date is the private collection’s own catalogue claim and has not been checked against the Nepalese (NGMCP) or Cambridge holdings; older manuscripts may survive in collections not yet catalogued online.

title: Rāma and Sītā are attested in more distinct texts in this graph than any deity
body:
Counting the distinct texts in which a figure is attested — directly, or through the passage a class-1 assertion cites — as on every profile page, Rāma (39), Sītā (26) and Kṛṣṇa (30) lead; Śiva and Viṣṇu are the strongest bridges in the network (highest betweenness), connecting otherwise separate corpora, temples and inscriptions.

Narrative figures travel across languages and religions — Hindu, Jain, Buddhist, Southeast Asian — where a deity’s cult is more often carried by temples and inscriptions than by retellings.
caveat: Network counts measure this dataset — which reflects what was researched — and are never evidence of religious importance or of historical truth.
